blocks.body:
The [[fta|fundamental theorem of arithmetic]] lets us sort integers by the shape of their factorisation. Three shapes come up again and again. Numbers all of whose prime factors are small (smooth numbers) are what factoring algorithms hunt for. Numbers in which every prime appears at least squared (powerful numbers) are where the abc conjecture has its bite. Numbers in which no prime appears twice (squarefree numbers) are the typical case and the support of the Möbius function.

For each class we ask: how many are there up to $x$? The answers are three quite different asymptotic laws, $\rho(u)x$, $c\sqrt x$ and $\frac6{\pi^2}x$, and each has a short proof that shows a useful technique.

blocks.title: Smooth, powerful and squarefree numbers
blocks.body:
Let $P(n)$ be the largest prime factor of $n$, with $P(1)=1$.
- $n$ is $y$-smooth if $P(n)\le y$. Write $\Psi(x,y)=\#\{n\le x:P(n)\le y\}$.
- $n$ is powerful (also called squarefull) if $p\mid n\Rightarrow p^2\mid n$ for every prime $p$.
- $n$ is squarefree if $p^2\nmid n$ for every prime $p$; equivalently $\mu(n)\ne0$.

The number $1$ belongs to all three classes. Smoothness depends on a parameter $y$; the other two are absolute properties of the exponents in the factorisation.

blocks.title: Squarefree numbers: inclusion–exclusion with squares
blocks.body:
Each $n\ge1$ can be written uniquely as $n=a^2b$ with $b$ squarefree: put each prime with an even exponent entirely into $a^2$, and for a prime with an odd exponent $e$ put $p^{e-1}$ into $a^2$ and $p$ into $b$. Then $d^2\mid n$ exactly when $d\mid a$, so by the basic property of the Möbius function ([[mobius]])
$$\sum_{d^2\mid n}\mu(d)=\sum_{d\mid a}\mu(d)=\begin{cases}1,&a=1,\\0,&a>1,\end{cases}$$
which is $1$ exactly when $n$ is squarefree. In other words $\mu(n)^2=\sum_{d^2\mid n}\mu(d)$. This is the sieve of Eratosthenes run with the squares $4,9,25,\dots$ instead of the primes.

blocks.title: Counting squarefree numbers
blocks.body:
Let $Q(x)$ be the number of squarefree $n\le x$. Then
$$Q(x)=\frac{6}{\pi^2}\,x+O(\sqrt x).$$

Sum the identity $\mu(n)^2=\sum_{d^2\mid n}\mu(d)$ over $n\le x$ and swap the order of summation. The multiples of $d^2$ up to $x$ number $\lfloor x/d^2\rfloor$, and only $d\le\sqrt x$ contribute:
$$Q(x)=\sum_{d\le\sqrt x}\mu(d)\Bigl\lfloor\frac{x}{d^2}\Bigr\rfloor=x\sum_{d\le\sqrt x}\frac{\mu(d)}{d^2}+O(\sqrt x),$$
since each floor differs from $x/d^2$ by less than $1$. The full series is $\sum_{d\ge1}\mu(d)d^{-2}=1/\zeta(2)=6/\pi^2$ ([[zeta]]), and the tail is $\bigl|\sum_{d>\sqrt x}\mu(d)d^{-2}\bigr|\le\sum_{d>\sqrt x}d^{-2}\le\frac{1}{\sqrt x-1}$ for $x>1$. Multiplying by $x$ gives another $O(\sqrt x)$.

blocks.title: Powerful numbers: a parametrisation
blocks.body: Powerful numbers are much rarer, about $\sqrt x$ of them up to $x$, because they are close to squares. Every square is powerful, and so is every number $a^2b^3$. Conversely, every powerful $n$ is of this form, and uniquely so if we insist that $b$ is squarefree: for each prime $p$ dividing $n$ with exponent $e\ge2$, if $e$ is even put $p^e$ into $a^2$; if $e$ is odd (so $e\ge3$) put $p^3$ into $b^3$ and $p^{e-3}$ into $a^2$. The squarefree $b$ must be the product of the primes appearing to an odd power, since in $a^2b^3$ the exponent of $p$ is $2v_p(a)+3[p\mid b]$, which is odd exactly when $p\mid b$. So $b$ and then $a$ are determined.

blocks.title: Counting powerful numbers
blocks.body:
Let $P_2(x)$ be the number of powerful $n\le x$. Then
$$P_2(x)=\frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\zeta(3)}\sqrt x+O(x^{1/3}),\qquad\frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\zeta(3)}\approx2.1733.$$

By the parametrisation, $P_2(x)$ counts pairs $(a,b)$ with $b$ squarefree and $a^2b^3\le x$. For fixed $b$ there are $\lfloor\sqrt{x/b^3}\rfloor$ choices of $a$, and $b\le x^{1/3}$. So
$$P_2(x)=\sum_{\substack{b\le x^{1/3}\\ b\text{ squarefree}}}\Bigl\lfloor\frac{\sqrt x}{b^{3/2}}\Bigr\rfloor=\sqrt x\sum_{\substack{b\le x^{1/3}\\ b\text{ squarefree}}}b^{-3/2}+O(x^{1/3}).$$
The series over all squarefree $b$ has Euler product $\prod_p(1+p^{-3/2})=\prod_p\frac{1-p^{-3}}{1-p^{-3/2}}=\frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\zeta(3)}$, and its tail beyond $x^{1/3}$ is at most $\sum_{b>x^{1/3}}b^{-3/2}\ll x^{-1/6}$, which contributes $O(\sqrt x\cdot x^{-1/6})=O(x^{1/3})$.

blocks.title: Smooth numbers and Dickman's function
blocks.body:
Now fix $u\ge1$ and count $n\le x$ with all prime factors at most $x^{1/u}$. The answer is a positive proportion of $x$, but the proportion falls very fast with $u$.

For $1\le u\le2$ it is easy. A number $n\le x$ can have at most one prime factor $p>x^{1/u}\ge\sqrt x$, since two would multiply to more than $x$. So the numbers that are not $x^{1/u}$-smooth are counted exactly once each by
$$x-\Psi(x,x^{1/u})=\sum_{x^{1/u}<p\le x}\Bigl\lfloor\frac xp\Bigr\rfloor=x\sum_{x^{1/u}<p\le x}\frac1p+O(\pi(x)).$$
By Mertens' theorem $\sum_{p\le t}\frac1p=\log\log t+M+O(1/\log t)$ ([[mertens]]), the sum of $1/p$ equals $\log\log x-\log\log x^{1/u}+o(1)=\log u+o(1)$. Since $\pi(x)=o(x)$, we get
$$\Psi(x,x^{1/u})=(1-\log u+o(1))\,x\qquad(1\le u\le2).$$
In particular about $1-\log2\approx30.7\%$ of integers have no prime factor above their square root.

For larger $u$ the same idea, applied recursively (remove the largest prime factor $p$ and count the cofactor, which is $p$-smooth and at most $x/p$), leads to the identity $\Psi(x,y)=\Psi(x,z)-\sum_{y<p\le z}\Psi(x/p,p)$ for $y<z$, and in the limit to a delay differential equation.

blocks.title: Dickman's theorem
blocks.body:
Let $\rho$ be the continuous function on $[0,\infty)$ with $\rho(u)=1$ for $0\le u\le1$ and
$$u\rho'(u)=-\rho(u-1)\qquad(u>1).$$
Then for every fixed $u\ge1$,
$$\Psi(x,x^{1/u})\sim\rho(u)\,x\qquad(x\to\infty).$$
Moreover $\rho(u)=u^{-u(1+o(1))}$ as $u\to\infty$.

blocks.title: The size of ρ and why factoring cares
blocks.body:
From the differential equation, $\rho(u)=1-\log u$ on $[1,2]$, and numerically
$$\rho(2)\approx0.3069,\quad\rho(3)\approx0.0486,\quad\rho(4)\approx0.00491,\quad\rho(5)\approx3.55\times10^{-4},\quad\rho(10)\approx2.77\times10^{-11}.$$
The rough rule $\rho(u)\approx u^{-u}$ explains the decay: a number is $x^{1/u}$-smooth roughly when it splits into $u$ pieces of size $x^{1/u}$, and each piece is a "coincidence" of probability about $1/u$.

An upper bound of the right flavour is easy (Rankin's trick): for any $\sigma>0$,
$$\Psi(x,y)\le\sum_{P(n)\le y}\Bigl(\frac xn\Bigr)^{\sigma}=x^{\sigma}\prod_{p\le y}\bigl(1-p^{-\sigma}\bigr)^{-1},$$
because each term with $n\le x$ is at least $1$ and the others are positive. Optimising $\sigma$ already gives bounds of the shape $x\,u^{-u(1+o(1))}$ in wide ranges.

Factoring. To factor $N$, the quadratic sieve looks for many $x$ such that $x^2-N$ (or $x^2\bmod N$) is $y$-smooth. Once there are more such numbers than primes up to $y$, linear algebra modulo $2$ finds a product that is a perfect square, giving $a^2\equiv b^2\pmod N$, and $\gcd(a-b,N)$ is often a proper factor. A larger $y$ makes smooth values more common but requires more of them; balancing the two with Dickman's function gives running time $\exp\bigl((1+o(1))\sqrt{\log N\log\log N}\bigr)$. The number field sieve uses smaller numbers to test for smoothness and reaches $\exp\bigl(O((\log N)^{1/3}(\log\log N)^{2/3})\bigr)$. The same smoothness counts govern index-calculus attacks on the [[discrete-log|discrete logarithm problem]] and hence the key sizes for [[rsa|RSA]].

blocks.title: Example 1: checking the laws at x = 10^6
blocks.body: Compare $Q(10^6)$ and $P_2(10^6)$ with the main terms of the theorems.
blocks.solution:
Direct counting gives $Q(10^6)=607926$, against $\frac6{\pi^2}10^6\approx607927.1$, an error of about $1$, far inside the $O(10^3)$ allowed.

For powerful numbers, $P_2(10^6)=2027$, against $\frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\zeta(3)}\cdot1000\approx2173.3$. The difference of about $-146$ is comparable to $x^{1/3}=100$, as the error term allows. In fact a finer analysis (Bateman and Grosswald) gives the second term $\frac{\zeta(2/3)}{\zeta(2)}x^{1/3}$, and $\zeta(2/3)\approx-2.447$ is negative; with it the prediction becomes $2173.3-148.8\approx2024.5$, within $3$ of the true count.

blocks.title: Example 2: smooth numbers converge slowly
blocks.body: Compute $\Psi(10^6,10^3)$ and $\Psi(10^6,10^2)$ and compare with $\rho(2)x$ and $\rho(3)x$.
blocks.solution:
A sieve for the largest prime factor gives $\Psi(10^6,1000)=344299$ and $\Psi(10^6,100)=72271$, that is $34.4\%$ and $7.2\%$, against $\rho(2)\approx30.7\%$ and $\rho(3)\approx4.9\%$.

The asymptotic is correct but the convergence is slow: the relative error behaves like a constant over $\log y$, and $\log 1000\approx6.9$ is small. For $u=3$ the true proportion is about $1.5$ times $\rho(3)$. In applications (for instance when tuning a factoring algorithm) one uses more precise approximations or computes $\Psi$ directly.

blocks.title: Example 3: consecutive powerful numbers
blocks.body: Show that there are infinitely many pairs of consecutive integers that are both powerful.
blocks.solution:
Consider [[pell|Pell's equation]] $x^2-8y^2=1$. It has the solution $(3,1)$, and from any solution $(x,y)$ we get the larger solution $(3x+8y,\,x+3y)$, since $(3x+8y)^2-8(x+3y)^2=x^2-8y^2$. So there are infinitely many solutions with $y\ge1$.

For each solution, $8y^2=2^3y^2$ is powerful: $2$ appears to an exponent at least $3$, and every other prime divides $y^2$ to an even, hence at least second, power. And $x^2=8y^2+1$ is a square, hence powerful. So $8y^2$ and $8y^2+1$ are consecutive powerful numbers. The first few pairs are $(8,9)$, $(288,289)$, $(9800,9801)$.

Erdős conjectured that there are no three consecutive powerful numbers; this is open.

blocks.title: Example 4: smoothness as a probability
blocks.body: Roughly what fraction of integers near $10^{100}$ have no prime factor above $10^{20}$? Compare $\rho(u)$ with the rule of thumb $u^{-u}$.
blocks.solution:
Here $u=\frac{\log10^{100}}{\log10^{20}}=5$, so Dickman's theorem suggests a proportion of about $\rho(5)\approx3.5\times10^{-4}$, about one in $2800$. The crude rule gives $5^{-5}=3.2\times10^{-4}$, the same order of magnitude. (Example 2 shows that the true proportion at finite height is somewhat larger than $\rho(u)$, but with $\log y\approx46$ the correction is much smaller than at $y=100$.)

So among random 100-digit numbers, smooth ones are rare but far from impossible to find; this is what makes the sieve methods practical.

blocks.body:
- Dickman's asymptotic is for fixed $u$ (that is, $y$ a fixed power of $x$). When $y$ is a power of $\log x$ the behaviour is different: $\Psi(x,(\log x)^A)=x^{1-1/A+o(1)}$ for fixed $A>1$.
- Powerful is not the same as being a perfect power: $72=2^3\cdot3^2$ is powerful but not a perfect power, and both classes have about $\sqrt x$ members up to $x$ but with different constants.
- The density of squarefree numbers is $\frac6{\pi^2}\approx0.608$, not $\prod_p(1-\frac1p)$, which is $0$. Squarefreeness restricts each prime a little ($1-p^{-2}$), not much.
- Do not plug finite $x$ into $\rho(u)x$ and expect accuracy (Example 2).
- $1$ is smooth, powerful and squarefree; formulas are stated with that convention.

The squarefree count is the simplest example of a sieve with Möbius weights ([[mobius]], [[sieve-basics]]); the constant is $1/\zeta(2)$ and the whole subject is driven by Euler products ([[zeta]]). Smooth number estimates rest on [[mertens|Mertens' theorems]] and are central to computational number theory: factoring, [[primality|primality testing]] analyses, [[rsa]] and the [[discrete-log|discrete logarithm]]. They are also an ingredient in constructing large gaps between primes ([[prime-patterns]]), where one needs few smooth numbers in an interval, and in [[probabilistic-nt|probabilistic number theory]], where the largest prime factor of a random integer has a limiting distribution described by $\rho$. Powerful numbers have small radical ($\mathrm{rad}(n)\le\sqrt n$), which is exactly what the abc conjecture controls; [[pell|Pell equations]] produce the consecutive pairs.

1. Show that the density of odd squarefree numbers is $\frac4{\pi^2}$.
2. Show that $\mathrm{rad}(n)\le\sqrt n$ for powerful $n$, where $\mathrm{rad}(n)$ is the product of the distinct primes dividing $n$, with equality exactly when $n$ is the square of a squarefree number.
3. Show that $\Psi(x,3)\sim\frac{(\log x)^2}{2\log2\log3}$.
4. Use the differential equation to write $\rho(u)$ on $[2,3]$ as an explicit integral, and evaluate $\rho(3)$ numerically.
